title: API versioning and compatibility
idea: Backward compatibility means clients built against an old version of your API keep working, unchanged, after you release a new one.
points: Additive changes are safe only for tolerant readers: optional fields, `default` methods.
Renames, removals and unit changes break callers; ship them as a new major version.
Readers should ignore unknown fields and default missing ones: the tolerant reader.
A version field lets one reader upcast old shapes and reject unknown future ones.

hero.caption: Silent breaks, such as a unit change, are the worst: nothing fails, but the numbers are wrong.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: A strict v1 consumer. One added field and one rename both take it down.

walk.text: Three producer releases: the original, one that adds `giftWrap`, one that renames `qty`.
The reader rejects any key it does not know, so a harmless addition breaks it.
Even past that check, a renamed `qty` would be missing here. Renames always break old readers.
Look at the output: only the first message survives. Every deploy of the producer is an outage.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: A versioned, tolerant reader accepts two schema versions and rejects an unknown future one loudly.

walk.text: A missing version means v1, so messages sent before versioning still parse.
`v` is bumped only for breaking changes. A newer one may mean anything, so fail loudly.
Upcasting maps the old name onto the new model in one place.
A required field that is absent fails with a clear message, not a raw null error.
`giftWrap` was added without a version bump; older producers omit it, so it defaults to false.
Unknown keys are skipped, so producers can add fields without a coordinated release.
The record still validates. Tolerance applies to shape, not to bad values.

pitfalls: Deleting a public method in a minor release; mark it `@Deprecated`, delegate, remove later.
Changing amounts from cents to dollars under the same field name; old clients misread silently.
Readers that reject unknown fields; every additive change on the producer becomes an outage.

quiz.q: Many teams implement your library's public `PaymentGateway` interface. You need to add `refund`. Which change keeps their code compiling?
options: Add refund as an abstract method
Add refund as a default method
Change the return type of charge to cover refunds
Rename the interface and delete the old one
quiz.why: A `default` method has a body, so existing implementations inherit it and still compile. An abstract method forces every implementer to change at once.

takeaway: Add freely, never rename or remove in place, and read tolerantly.
